summary: Describes the policy for registering second-level domains under the .MIL domain. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes who could register a name directly under .MIL and how to apply. It also sets requirements for names and supporting name servers.

questions: how to register a mil domain
who may register a mil domain
subtitle: The 1996 policy for registering second-level names under .MIL.

tldr.problem: The memo sets out who may register second-level domains under .MIL and how those domains are administered.
tldr.mechanism: It assigns administration to the DoD NIC, limits direct registration to specified US military and DoD organizations, and sets naming and name-server requirements.
tldr.outcome: It records an Informational policy for .MIL registration; the memo does not claim a later or current status.

today: RFC 1956 is an Informational memo published in June 1996. Its text records the .MIL registration policy described above.

sections.title: Administration of the .MIL Domain
sections.content:
The RFC says the .MIL domain is delegated from the root authority to the US Department of Defense. The DoD Network Information Center (NIC) administers the domain.

The memo describes registration policy for second-level names under .MIL. It is informational and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The US Department of Defense is responsible for .MIL. Its Network Information Center handles the domain's administration.

sections.title: Who May Register Directly
sections.content:
Only US military services, unified or specified commands, and DoD operating agencies outside military service chains may register directly as second-level .MIL domains. Other DoD organizations must register through the second-level domain administrators for their respective organizations.

Names should describe the organization they serve, should preferably be no longer than 12 characters, and must be unique. If names collide, the RFC specifies first come, first served.
sections.plainLanguage: Only certain military services and DoD bodies can register directly under .MIL. Other DoD groups use their organization's domain administrators.

sections.title: Name Servers and the Application
sections.content:
Each second-level .MIL domain must have at least two name servers; placing them on separate networks is preferred. All DNS servers that support .MIL subdomains must themselves be in .MIL.

Applicants use the template supplied by the DoD NIC and send it to the DoD NIC hostmaster. The hostmaster accepts templates only from registered .MIL users.
sections.plainLanguage: Each domain needs at least two name servers, preferably on separate networks. A registered .MIL user must submit the registration template.
